raw_case_text:
A 61-year-old immunocompetent woman presented with a chronic headache for 10 months that had been progressively worsening for 18 days with emesis. She had an irregular headache without relation to body, position, or time. The patient was a peasant with no particular exposure to avian (especially pigeon) feces or woodworking. The headache got worse, with several nonbloody, nonbilious vomiting episodes, and the patient developed an ataxic gait 18 days before hospital admission. A comprehensive physical examination of her body at admission did not show any pertinent findings. There was no evidence of compromised immunological function or signs of localized infection. She could not complete the hand alternating movement test, her right side of finger-nose test was positive, and her heel-knee-tibia test was suspiciously positive, but Romberg's sign was negative. The rest of the physical examination did not present any abnormalities. Blood cell count, urine analysis, and blood biochemistry were normal. HIV antibody test was repeatedly negative. Gram stain and India ink stain of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) were negative. CSF and blood were negative for cultures. The cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test of CSF was negative the first time, but it was positive the second time; the titer was 1:32.
Abdominal and chest radiographs were negative. A plain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the head demonstrated a 26x21x16 mm3 nodule as long or equal to T1 and long T2 signal in the right cerebellar hemisphere with no adjacent edema, and the nodule was significantly enhanced as nodular with a thick and annular wall after contrast administration (Figure 1C-E). There was no midline shift, and the compression of adjacent structures was not apparent (Figure 1A and B). The patient was considered to have a metastatic tumor or glioma in the right cerebellar hemisphere.
The cerebellar nodule was removed by neurosurgery via a suboccipital craniotomy in the left lateral position. An 80 mm long straight incision was made 20 mm outside the right side of the occipital bone of the lower lateral hairline. Intraoperatively, the lower part of the transverse sinus and the surface layer of cerebellum were exposed. Subcortical dissection was performed until a 40x30x20 mm firm nodule with moderate vascular supply and distinct border was identified, located at the upper portion of the right cerebellar hemisphere. The blood vessels that supply for the nodule were cut off by electrocoagulation, and then en bloc resection of the nodule along the border was performed.
A portion of the nodule was sent for pathologic analysis. A large number of mononuclear cells and multinucleated giant cells were seen, with diffused distribution. There was a small amount of bacteria circular structure and mesenchyme hyalinization, with a large number of lymphocytes and a few plasma cell infiltrations; local tissue necrosis with neutrophil infiltration was also found in the frozen section tissues (Figure 1F). Immunohistochemical staining yielded CD68 (+), cytokeratin (-), epithelial membrane antigen (-), glial fibrillary acidic protein (-), Ki-67 (-), neurofilament(-), neuron-specific enolase (-), soluble-protein 100 (-), vimentin (+), cluster of differentiation 1a (-), and thallus periodic acid-schiff stain (+). The neuropathology evidenced a right cerebellar cryptococcal granuloma.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 61-year-old immunocompetent female peasant presented with a 10-month history of chronic irregular headache that worsened over the preceding 18 days with non-bilious vomiting and ataxic gait.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had experienced an irregular headache unrelated to posture or time of day for 10 months. Eighteen days prior to admission, the headache progressively worsened and was accompanied by multiple episodes of non-bloody, non-bilious vomiting and gait ataxia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Immunocompetent peasant with no history of immunodeficiency, localized infection, woodworking, or exposure to avian/pigeon feces.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic worsening headache, non-bloody non-bilious vomiting, and gait ataxia.

objective.physical_examination: General physical examination was normal. Neurological examination revealed ataxic gait, inability to complete the rapid alternating hand movement test (dysdiadochokinesia), positive right finger-to-nose test, suspiciously positive heel-knee-shin test, and negative Romberg's sign.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count, urinalysis, blood biochemistry, blood cultures, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal; HIV antibody testing was repeatedly negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial CSF Gram stain, India ink stain, fungal/bacterial cultures, and first CSF cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test were negative, while a repeat CSF cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination test was positive at a titer of 1:32. Brain MRI revealed a 26 x 21 x 16 mm T1-isointense/hypointense, T2-hyperintense nodule in the right cerebellar hemisphere with thick annular contrast enhancement and no perilesional edema or midline shift (initially suspected to be a metastasis or glioma). Suboccipital craniotomy with en bloc resection of the 40 x 30 x 20 mm firm right cerebellar mass and histopathology/immunohistochemistry showed granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells, lymphocytes, plasma cells, focal necrosis, CD68(+), vimentin(+), PAS(+) fungal organisms, and negative CK, EMA, GFAP, Ki-67, NF, NSE, S-100, and CD1a.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of solitary right cerebellar cryptococcal granuloma (cryptococcoma) in an immunocompetent patient, confirmed by repeat CSF cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination titer of 1:32 and neuropathological examination with periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positive fungal staining following suboccipital craniotomy and en bloc resection; glioma and metastatic carcinoma were excluded by immunohistochemistry.
